package_info.why_malicious: The Qakbot DLL is designed to establish persistence on infected Windows systems by abusing legitimate system processes (srtasks.exe), employs anti-analysis techniques, hides its components, and enables remote command execution and credential theft. It is distributed via phishing campaigns and is part of a well-known botnet infrastructure.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after DLL is loaded by srtasks.exe)
execution_context.file_location: malicious DLL file dropped by phishing campaign

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: DLL code that hijacks srtasks.exe for persistence and injects malicious payloads into memory, evading detection.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the DLL is loaded by srtasks.exe, establishes persistence by registering itself to run at system startup, injects malicious payloads into memory, and communicates with remote C2 servers for further instructions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hijacking a legitimate Windows process (srtasks.exe) for persistence and code execution is a common malware tactic to evade detection and maintain access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal DLLs loaded by srtasks.exe should not establish persistence, inject code, or communicate with external servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software may use DLLs for extending functionality, but not for persistence or process injection.
key_indicators: DLL loaded by srtasks.exe (unusual for legitimate software)
Process injection and in-memory payload execution

execution_context.file_location: malicious dropper (phishing email attachment or download)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Dropper code that unpacks and loads the malicious DLL, deletes itself after execution, and employs anti-analysis techniques.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the dropper unpacks the malicious DLL, loads it into srtasks.exe, deletes itself from disk to evade forensic analysis, and checks for virtualized or sandboxed environments to avoid detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-deleting droppers and anti-analysis checks are hallmarks of sophisticated malware aiming to evade detection and hinder analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers or updaters do not delete themselves or check for sandboxes/virtual machines.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters may remove old versions, but not in this stealthy manner.

attack_chain.action: Victim receives phishing email with IRS-themed lure and malicious attachment or link.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of dropper on victim's machine

attack_chain.action: Dropper is executed, unpacks and loads the malicious Qakbot DLL, then deletes itself to evade detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious DLL is loaded by srtasks.exe

attack_chain.action: Malicious DLL establishes persistence via srtasks.exe, injects payloads, and initiates C2 communication.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing system compromise, credential theft, and remote control

behavioral_signatures: DLL loaded by srtasks.exe that establishes persistence
Process injection and in-memory payload execution
file_indicators: Unexpected DLLs in locations associated with srtasks.exe
Temporary dropper files that disappear after execution
network_indicators: Outbound connections from srtasks.exe to known Qakbot C2 domains/IPs
Encrypted or obfuscated C2 traffic patterns
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for DLLs loaded by srtasks.exe that are not signed by Microsoft, especially those establishing persistence or injecting code. Look for process creation events where srtasks.exe spawns network connections or loads unexpected modules. Detect self-deleting executables and anti-analysis logic in new binaries. Correlate with phishing email delivery and IRS-themed lures.
